items.title: Mcbee interviewed by Monk Rowe, 2020
items.q: the very next year I joined the Charles Lloyd Quartet.

ctx.x: Well as you said, your older guys who have been around, when you moved to New York in 1964, I think I’m correct about that, I’m going to guess that as a jazz musician you had to do a certain amount of scrambling, reaching out to other people, finding a mentor, and making connections. Isn’t that part of finding out who you are, forming your personality. And I wonder if young people don’t have that opportunity now?

Young people don’t have a lot of that kind of opportunity, but as far as I’m concerned, when I arrived in New York City I needed not a sound. I had no need for a mentor. I had no need to discover myself. I had, although having not researched who was doing what at what level, etcetera, etcetera. I had studied. I wanted to be a music teacher. So I finished college before arriving in New York and I tell everybody that in college I flunked everything but I was a great student in the music area. And so when I arrived…

instrument, I mean I was in the Army before I finished college, in the band, as a clarinetist. And when the band practices were finished, for two years, I would practice my bass throughout the waning, the late hours of the evening, on and on. You know I had this inspiration to develop my personal reality. So doing that for two years, then returning to college, finishing, graduating with a degree in music education, when I arrived in New York City I felt I had something on my shoulder. And upon listening to those…

items.title: Mcbee interviewed by Monk Rowe, 2020
items.q: By now I’m playing literally around the world with Keith Jarrett, Jack DeJohnette, and Charles Lloyd.

ctx.x: Okay. Enough said. I want to talk — we’re getting time to wrap up here and I so enjoy our conversations. I wanted to ask you about song titles and how they relate to the sound of the music and the intent of the music. We talked a little bit and we mentioned some of Pharoah Sanders’ pieces and Alice Coltrane. Now with your own compositions, do you have titles in mind before you start or does something sort of come to you as the song progresses?

Good question. Excuse me. I might have mentioned before that currently, given this Covid situation, I’ve been working on four compositions. Some tunes, one tune I’ll work on today — to limits, to find limits. Then I might go to another one tomorrow. I’m almost completed. But what I do is, since the very beginning, that is my first composition in New York was a tune called “Song of Her” we mentioned that before. It’s from the second side of the “Forest Flower” album, recorded by Charles Lloyd. There was a moment…

tone alone. And in response to not only what it prevails but it might advance notice crossing the bar line into another situation. So you might want to make changes as you go along you know, instead of using a ninth or a fifth, I might use a sixth that might go down to a two and then, you know, etcetera etcetera. So once the tune is completed then it’s time to name the tune. I’ve got a list of names that come to me occasionally that I’ve written back there in my studio, but none have found worth to these three…
